title: The Common Gateway Interface (CGI) Version 1.1
summary: Specifies the Common Gateway Interface version 1.1, a simple, platform-independent way for an information server, in practice an HTTP server, to run external programs and pass them a request. The interface has been used by the Web since 1993, and this document records it.

plainLanguage.summary: When a web server cannot answer by itself, it can call a small helper program and pass back its answer. This document says how they talk.

questions: how do cgi scripts get request data
what meta-variables are passed to a cgi script
how does a cgi script send output back to the web server
subtitle: How web servers run helper programs and pass them request data.

tldr.problem: A web server cannot answer every request by itself; it needs a way to invoke external programs and pass them the details of the client request.
tldr.mechanism: CGI defines a set of environment variables and conventions that the server uses to tell the program what the client wants, how to read request data, and where to write the response.
tldr.outcome: The web has relied on CGI since 1993 to power dynamic content. Although newer technologies have emerged, CGI remains widely used and this RFC records the current practice.

facts.label: Core concept
facts.value: Environment variables passed from server to script

facts.label: Request data method
facts.value: Standard input for POST; environment variables for GET/HEAD

today: RFC 3875 is Informational and remains current. CGI 1.1 is the standard for HTTP server-script interaction, though newer technologies like FastCGI, Perl modules for Apache, and application frameworks have reduced reliance on raw CGI for new deployments. The specification is used as a reference by servers and script developers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
CGI (Common Gateway Interface) is the bridge between an HTTP server and external programs. The server receives a client request, invokes a CGI script (the helper program), passes it information about the request through environment variables and standard input, and returns the script's response to the client.

The server handles network and transport issues; the script handles the application logic. CGI has been the de facto standard for this since 1993 when the World-Wide Web began at the U.S. National Centre for Supercomputing Applications.
sections.plainLanguage: A web server gets a request and says to a helper program: here is what the user asked for. The helper runs, figures out the answer, and the server sends it back.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
Meta-variables are the core of CGI: named parameters that the server sets and the script reads. They carry information from the server to the script: who is asking (REMOTE_ADDR), what they are asking for (REQUEST_METHOD and PATH_INFO), what data they sent (CONTENT_LENGTH and CONTENT_TYPE). The script accesses them in a system-defined way, usually as environment variables.

A script in CGI is any executable program: a compiled binary, a shell script, a Perl or Python program, or even a library function linked into the server. The term does not imply interpretation at run-time.
sections.plainLanguage: Meta-variables are like labels on a package: who sent it, where to send the answer, what's inside. The server fills them in and the script reads them to know what to do.

sections.title: Request Meta-Variables
sections.content:
The RFC defines 17 standard meta-variables. Essential ones include:

  • REQUEST_METHOD: the HTTP method (GET, POST, HEAD, or others).
  • SCRIPT_NAME and PATH_INFO: the path to the script and any extra path information the script may interpret.
  • QUERY_STRING: data from a GET request or form submission, URL-encoded.
  • CONTENT_TYPE and CONTENT_LENGTH: the type and size of data sent by the client in the request body.
  • REMOTE_ADDR and REMOTE_HOST: the client's IP address and hostname.
  • SERVER_NAME and SERVER_PORT: the server's hostname and port.
  • AUTH_TYPE and REMOTE_USER: authentication information if the server enforced authentication.

Protocol-specific meta-variables like HTTP_ACCEPT mirror HTTP header fields. Servers may add implementation-defined extensions prefixed with X_.
sections.plainLanguage: The server fills in variables like the client's address, what method they used, the path they asked for, and what data they sent. The script reads these to know what happened.

sections.title: Request and Response
sections.content:
The server invokes the script and makes request data available. If the REQUEST_METHOD is GET or HEAD, parameters are in the QUERY_STRING and command-line arguments. If it is POST, the body data is available via standard input; the script reads up to CONTENT_LENGTH bytes.

The script writes its response to standard output: header fields followed by a blank line, then the message body. The response header must include a Content-Type field stating the media type. A Status field can specify an HTTP status code; without it, 200 OK is assumed.

For a local redirect, the script returns a Location header with a path; the server re-processes that request. For a client redirect, the script returns a Location header with an absolute URI; the server sends a 302 Found to the client.
sections.plainLanguage: The script reads what the server set up, figures out the answer, and writes back some header lines and then the content. The server takes that and sends it to the client.

sections.title: Security and Operational Guidelines
sections.content:
Since a script runs under the same user and privileges as the server, it must be trusted not to corrupt server files or configuration. The RFC cautions scripts against buffer overflows in parsing PATH_INFO or other data; it recommends rejecting requests with oversized components or validating input carefully before passing it to system calls, database commands, or other sensitive operations.

The RFC notes that REMOTE_ADDR and REMOTE_HOST may not identify the ultimate source if proxies are involved. Sensitive data should go in POST bodies, not in the URI where it may be logged. Scripts must check REQUEST_METHOD before attempting to process request data.

GET and HEAD should be idempotent and safe; POST may have side effects. For non-parsed-header (NPH) scripts, the server passes all responsibility for the HTTP response to the script, which must construct the complete response including the HTTP version line.
sections.plainLanguage: Scripts must be careful: they run with the server's powers and can damage it. They should check the data they get, reject anything too big or strange, and never trust client input.
